interactions: Cyclobenzaprine + hydrocodone + methocarbamol: additive CNS depression; cyclobenzaprine is anticholinergic. Together with tamsulosin (alpha-1 blockade) they increase the risk of orthostatic hypotension and falls.
Hydrocodone: opioid miosis can mask pupillary signs.
Ibuprofen and acetaminophen: antipyretic effect can mask fever. Ibuprofen + lisinopril: risk of acute kidney injury, greater during sepsis and hypovolaemia.
Dexamethasone + metformin: corticosteroids raise blood glucose; monitor capillary glucose and use insulin as needed.
Metformin: risk of lactic acidosis in sepsis with raised lactate (2.8 mmol/L); withhold during the acute illness.
Ceftriaxone and ampicillin: no clinically significant interaction with the current medicines; no renal dose adjustment at eGFR about 70.
output.proposed: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours + ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours + dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours. Current medicines: lisinopril 20 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, methocarbamol 750 mg three times daily as needed, acetaminophen/hydrocodone 325/5 mg every 6 hours as needed, cyclobenzaprine 10 mg three times daily, ibuprofen 400 mg every 8 hours as needed, tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily. No known drug allergies. Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL (eGFR about 70 mL/min/1.73m2, CKD-EPI 2021).

prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.

Do not delay lumbar puncture or antibiotics to obtain a CT head: cranial imaging is not routine before lumbar puncture (WHO 2025 section A.4; NICE NG240 1.4.6) and no imaging-first criterion is present.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
Do NOT assume a benign musculoskeletal etiology for persistent neck stiffness with tachycardia and leukocytosis without first excluding meningitis with LP and a cervical spinal infection with MRI.
required_recommendations: Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.4.1 and 1.6.3). Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).
Add ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours for Listeria monocytogenes cover because of diabetes mellitus (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.6.6).

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3). Stop dexamethasone on identification of Streptococcus agalactiae (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3).
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.

Proceed to lumbar puncture without prior cranial imaging: no WHO 2025 section A.4 criterion is present (GCS 15, no focal signs, no cranial nerve deficit, no papilloedema, no new seizure, not severely immunocompromised). Age, confusion and diabetes are not imaging criteria.
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: high-dose penicillin G (4 million units IV every 4 hours) or ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours for Streptococcus agalactiae, for 14 days (NICE NG240), longer if a deep focus is found; gentamicin may be added for synergy in the first 5 to 7 days.

Obtain contrast-enhanced MRI of the cervical spine to exclude cervical epidural abscess, vertebral osteomyelitis and septic facet arthritis (15 days of torticollis, focal left paraspinal tenderness, streptococcal bacteraemia).
Treat the right lower-extremity venous stasis ulcer as the portal of entry: inspect it, culture the cleaned ulcer bed, and arrange wound care and debridement as needed for source control.

Withhold cyclobenzaprine, methocarbamol, hydrocodone and ibuprofen, which confound the assessment and contributed to near-syncope, and withhold metformin during sepsis; monitor glucose on dexamethasone.
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.

Bacterial meningitis can present without fever or headache, particularly in older or diabetic patients and under antipyretic analgesics (here acetaminophen and ibuprofen); persistent neck stiffness with tachycardia, WBC 34.5 and CRP 185 warrants lumbar puncture.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.1).

Proceed to lumbar puncture without prior cranial imaging: no WHO 2025 section A.4 criterion is present (GCS 15, no focal signs, no cranial nerve deficit, no papilloedema, no new seizure, not severely immunocompromised). Age, confusion and diabetes are not imaging criteria.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3).

A negative Gram stain does not exclude bacterial meningitis: sensitivity is about 85% with wide confidence limits (WHO 2025), lower after antibiotics; culture and multiplex PCR establish the organism.
A CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.4 or less is abnormally low (WHO 2025 A.2.2) and is more informative than the absolute value, above all in hyperglycaemia.

Empirical therapy is ceftriaxone or cefotaxime within 60 minutes, with ampicillin when a Listeria risk factor (age over 60, pregnancy, immunocompromise) is present; vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance is locally prevalent (WHO 2025). Diabetes is counted as a Listeria risk factor in this benchmark.

Streptococcus agalactiae meningitis is uncommon in non-pregnant adults; diabetes, older age, malignancy, cirrhosis and skin and soft-tissue breaks are recognised risk factors and portals. Here the right lower-extremity venous stasis ulcer is the presumed portal of entry. Targeted therapy is penicillin G or ampicillin.

Torticollis with focal paraspinal tenderness and bacteraemia requires contrast MRI of the cervical spine: a non-contrast CT cannot exclude epidural abscess, vertebral osteomyelitis or septic facet arthritis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A negative Gram stain does not exclude bacterial meningitis: sensitivity is about 85% with wide confidence limits (WHO 2025); culture and multiplex PCR establish the organism (here S. agalactiae on the panel).
red_herrings.intended_effect: Lower the index of suspicion for bacterial meningitis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mild hyponatraemia (134 mEq/L) is common in bacterial meningitis and sepsis; it does not point away from meningitis and needs monitoring, not a separate endocrine work-up.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Redirect workup toward primary endocrine or volume-status causes of hyponatremia.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Gerald Novak is a 59-year-old right-handed retired warehouse manager who presents to the emergency department after a near-syncopal episode earlier today. His symptoms began 15 days ago with the insidious onset of neck stiffness, which he initially attributed to sleeping in an awkward position. He visited his primary care physician five days into his symptoms and was prescribed methocarbamol for presumed musculoskeletal neck pain. Despite the muscle relaxant, his symptoms did not improve. Two days later, he presented to this emergency department reporting involuntary contractions of the neck muscles causing his head to be held in left rotation. At that initial ED visit, he denied headache, photophobia, fever, nausea, vomiting, upper-extremity weakness or numbness, stridor, dysphagia, drooling, odynophagia, or respiratory symptoms. He had no history of trauma. He was afebrile with normal vital signs, and imaging of the head and cervical spine was obtained. He reported significant pain relief after receiving intramuscular ketorolac and was discharged with Tylenol #3 and instructions for primary care follow-up. Four days later he returned to the ED with persistent neck pain. He remained afebrile, his examination was unchanged, and he was treated with ketorolac and discharged with acetaminophen/hydrocodone, cyclobenzaprine, and ibuprofen. Today, four days after his second ED visit, he experienced a near-syncopal episode upon standing from a seated position. He reports feeling dizzy and lightheaded, which he attributes to the cyclobenzaprine. He again denies headache, fever, chills, nausea, or vomiting. His wife reports that he has seemed more fatigued over the past several days and has had a poor appetite. She notes that his neck has remained persistently stiff and twisted despite multiple medications. On arrival to the ED, he is tachycardic at 120 beats per minute but afebrile.
